control_audit.criterion: a control changes only comment or docstring text, or renames a local consistently to a name bound nowhere else (builtins count as bindings); anything touching an operator, keyword, numeric or string literal is a mutation

gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: The class docstring promises `cat-file -t` names the type without peeling, so "a tag or tree the document named is not the commit it named, and the resolver does not guess which commit it meant." Every proposed tree mutation attacks what happens AFTER _ready returns None (blob modes, size caps, symlinks, the digest case) plus one _ready reason-swap (missing git binary). Nobody attacks the gate that decides whether a named object is a commit at all. Weakened, a document naming an annotated-tag or tree id resolves silently against whatever git peels it to — the verdict stops being a function of the commit the document named, with no reason string to show for it.

A module-level dict keyed by (resolved repo path, commit) is the only thing binding a prereg: content-address answer to the commit the document names. The whole proposed set treats GitTree as stateless — not one mutation touches the cache. Drop the commit from the key and the second document verified in the same process gets the FIRST document's tree index: a prereg:SHA256 resolves to bytes that are not in the tree it named, HELD, no reason, no crash. This is the loudest available violation of "AT ONE COMMIT, never the working tree" and it is completely unprobed.

The study proposed the find_sha256 twin ("MemoryTree.find_sha256 answers with no commit named") and stopped. The rule — a handle that names no commit yields no evidence — is enforced independently in both methods, and only one of the two sites is under test. The path: form is the more commonly exercised of the two, so the untested half is the one more documents depend on.

The two SnapshotTree proposals reach the mode question through blob() (executable mode) and through size inference. find_sha256 re-implements the mode check inline as a separate conjunct; nothing in the proposed set touches that line. It is the one place where a symlink, gitlink or tree entry's embedded bytes can answer a content-addressed prereg: receipt, and the docstring specifically promises those three modes are not_a_blob "whatever bytes they carry."

gaps_after_the_critic.area: load_sidecar's tag-grammar guard on span receipt/kind (_ATTR_VALUE)
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: This is the sidecar layer's injection boundary: it is the ONLY check standing between a hostile sidecar and render() splicing a receipt string containing a double quote or `<` back into the document as extra sworn tags. Eleven sidecar mutations were proposed and every one of them is about offsets, ordering, keys, specs, or digests — none about the character content of the two attributes that get interpolated into bytes. `render` is a CLI subcommand of its own, so nothing downstream re-checks it.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: load_sidecar's upper bound on a span end offset (`b <= len(text)`)
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: The proposals cover the emptiness of the range, its ordering, its overlap and its UTF-8 boundary, but not whether it lies inside the text at all. Python slicing clamps, so an out-of-range end makes render() emit a document whose span table no longer describes it — silently, with no exception, on the standalone render path where verify()'s re-scan reconciliation never runs.

This is the single most load-bearing refusal in the module: the whole "trust neither the author nor the verifier that issued it" doctrine reduces to that one `and`. Every proposed receipt mutation attacks an INPUT to one of the two conjuncts — what goes in the digest, which schema branch fires, which build hash is compared, which manifest wins — and not one attacks the join. Weakened to digest_ok alone, re-derivation stops mattering entirely: a receipt that is internally consistent but describes a different document than the one presented still reports VERIFIED.

Three named commitments live in four lines and no proposed mutation touches any of them: `sworn_total_counts_malformed` (a MALFORMED span must deny SWORN-HELD), the module's stated rule that "a document that swore nothing is UNSWORN, never 'no failures'", and `document_malformed_is_failed`. Both weakenings are silent upgrades of the headline verdict — the field a reader actually acts on — and neither changes a single span verdict, so a suite that only asserts per-span outcomes will not notice.

Twelve coverage mutations were proposed; they cover the mask, the fences, the splitter, the whitespace, the rounding, the 0/0 case and the DIFF-CLAIM denominator (`d2`), but not the sentence-share denominator itself. Because sworn spans are masked out of the narrative before splitting, dropping sworn_total from the denominator inflates the floor on every document that actually swore something — precisely the direction of the v0.1 flattery R8 was written to withdraw, and the one number that survives into the CLI headline as `coverage-floor≈`.

gaps_after_the_critic.area: Not mutated but worth naming: coverage's binding is advisory by construction
gaps_after_the_critic.why_it_matters: `coverage_reproduces` is computed and then never consulted by `status`, so no mutation to issue_receipt's `coverage_sha256` can change a VERIFIED/FAILED outcome — R9's "coverage travels beside it under its own coverage_sha256" is unenforced by design. Similarly, `_v0_shape`'s projection can only be mutated in the loud direction (any key dropped from one side and not the other makes every v0 receipt FAIL), so the v0 comparison shape cannot be silently widened by a single-site edit. Both are structural facts about the layer, not gaps a mutation can measure — a study reporting per-layer defended-fractions should say so rather than let them read as passing.

mutations.name: R9 reversed: coverage is pulled back inside the digest
mutations.why: This one tuple IS the R9 decision. With "coverage" removed, issue_receipt digests the core WITH coverage, verify_receipt's v1 digest_body includes coverage, and the v1 comparison core carries coverage while cmp_fresh still drops it. A receipt whose coverage block was edited after issuance now reports digest_match False instead of VERIFIED-with-coverage_reproduces-False, and a well-formed round trip stops re-deriving at all. A test notices by asserting that editing receipt["coverage"] leaves status VERIFIED and only flips coverage_reproduces, and that digest == sha256(jcs(receipt minus digest/timestamp/coverage/coverage_sha256)).

mutations.name: a receipt with no schema field is verified instead of refused
mutations.new: if schema is not None and schema not in RECEIPT_SCHEMAS:
mutations.why: Drops the refusal for the one shape most likely to be forged: a receipt that names no schema at all. It falls through with v0 False, gets digested and compared under v1 rules, and can come back VERIFIED with schema None. A test notices by feeding a receipt with the schema key deleted (not merely set to an unknown string) and asserting FAILED plus "unknown receipt schema" in the note.

mutations.name: the schema-aware v0 branch never fires
mutations.why: Collapses M7's key-on-the-schema-string behaviour: a /v0 receipt in history is now digested over its body minus the v1 exclusion tuple (not minus digest/timestamp), compared on the full v1 shape instead of the projected v0 shape, and has its pre-sworn/coverage/1 coverage block compared as if it were current. Every committed v0 receipt turns FAILED. A test notices by verifying an actual committed /v0 receipt and asserting VERIFIED, coverage_reproduces is None, and "/v0 receipt" in the note.

mutations.name: an unserialisable receipt body passes the digest check
mutations.why: Turns the safe-default on a JCS failure inside out. A receipt carrying a value the canonicaliser cannot serialise (a non-string key, a NaN, a nested non-JSON type) is now treated as having a matching digest, so digest_match is True on a body that was never hashed. A test notices by handing verify_receipt a receipt with a poisoned field and asserting digest_match is False and status FAILED rather than merely 'does not crash'.

mutations.name: the coverage advisory is computed for v0 receipts and skipped for v1
mutations.old: if not v0 and isinstance(receipt.get("coverage"), dict):
mutations.why: Swaps the two schema branches for the advisory field. A v1 receipt now always reports coverage_reproduces None, so an edited coverage block is invisible; a v0 receipt reports False for a coverage block the docstring says cannot reproduce under this verifier. A test notices by asserting coverage_reproduces is True on a fresh v1 receipt, False after mutating its coverage, and None for a v0 receipt.

mutations.name: same_verifier_build keys on the version string, not the build hash
mutations.why: The verifier block names the build by hashing sworn.py precisely because the version string does not move on every edit. Keyed on styxx_version, a receipt issued by a patched sworn.py at the same version reports same_verifier_build True, hiding exactly the difference the field exists to report. A test notices by overwriting receipt["verifier"]["sworn_sha256"], re-issuing, and asserting same_verifier_build is False while status stays VERIFIED.

mutations.name: the sidecar-commit vs --commit disagreement is no longer refused
mutations.new: if commit is not None and sidecar["commit"] is None:
mutations.old: if commit is not None and sidecar["commit"] not in (None, commit):
mutations.why: Two changes in one guard: a sidecar naming commit A verified with --commit B is now accepted silently (the next line overwrites commit with the sidecar's, so the caller's flag is ignored without a word), and a commit-less sidecar given an explicit --commit is refused instead. Path receipts then resolve at a commit the caller did not authorise. A test notices by calling verify(sidecar=side, commit=other40) and asserting SystemExit mentioning both shas, and by asserting a commit-less sidecar plus an explicit commit does NOT refuse.

mutations.name: a supplied manifest that disagrees with the embedded one is accepted
mutations.new: if manifest is not None and manifest.digest_or_none() is None:
mutations.old: if manifest is not None and manifest.digest_or_none() != embedded.digest_or_none():
mutations.why: Removes the disagreement refusal: a caller can hand verify() a manifest whose receipts differ from the ones sealed into the sidecar, and since `manifest = manifest or embedded` keeps the supplied object, every span is adjudicated against the attacker's numbers while the sidecar's embedded manifest is silently discarded. The verdict core still reports manifest_digest, so nothing downstream sees the substitution. A test notices by building a sidecar with an embedded manifest and passing a differently-valued manifest, asserting SystemExit "the supplied manifest disagrees with the embedded one".

mutations.name: the re-scan span-table check stops caring about span order
mutations.why: `want` is the sidecar's span table in the order the sidecar wrote it; `seen` is sorted because the lexer's order is canonical. Comparing sorted-to-sorted accepts a sidecar whose spans are listed in an order the canonical form does not produce, so render/re-scan no longer pins the table's order and a sidecar can carry a permuted span list that renders to different-looking JSON while still verifying. A test notices by permuting sidecar["spans"] and asserting SystemExit "re-scanning the rendered sidecar does not reproduce its spans".

mutations.name: a tree handle keeps its own commit when the document names none
mutations.why: The comment two lines above states the rule: a document that names no commit gets no commit however the handle was built. With the fallback, a sidecar or inline document with commit None is adjudicated against whatever commit the GitTree handle happened to be constructed at, so path receipts resolve at a commit the document never named while core["commit"] still reports None. A test notices by verifying a commit-less document with a tree built at a real sha and asserting tree.commit is None afterwards (and that path spans come back UNRESOLVED, not HELD).

mutations.name: GitTree.blob stops treating a symlink as not_a_blob
mutations.old: if len(meta) < 4 or meta[1] != b"blob" or meta[0] == b"120000":
mutations.why: git ls-tree reports a symlink with object type `blob` and mode 120000, so the mode clause is the ONLY thing that stops a symlink from resolving. With it gone, `path:link` resolves and the symlink's target-path text is served as the receipt bytes: a document could point a quote or a JSON pointer at a link and have the link's target string verified as if it were a committed file. The reason vocabulary loses not_a_blob for the symlink case entirely. A test would have to build a git fixture containing a symlink (git update-index --add --cacheinfo 120000, or a real symlink on a platform that has them), commit it, and assert GitTree(repo, sha).blob("link") == (None, "not_a_blob"). The existing not_a_blob GitTree case uses a directory, which the meta[1] != b"blob" clause still catches, so nothing currently distinguishes the two clauses.

mutations.name: GitTree._index lets symlink blobs into the prereg index
mutations.old: if len(meta) >= 3 and meta[1] == b"blob" and meta[0] != b"120000":
mutations.why: The same blob-mode gate, on the prereg-by-digest path. With the mode clause dropped, a symlink's object is hashed into the sha256->oid index, so a `prereg:<digest>` receipt whose digest matches the symlink's TARGET TEXT resolves HELD instead of UNRESOLVED prereg_not_in_tree. An attacker who cannot commit a prereg file can commit a symlink whose name-bytes hash to the digest they want to claim. A test would have to commit a symlink whose target string is the prereg body and assert GitTree(repo, sha).find_sha256(sha256(target_bytes)) == (None, "prereg_not_in_tree"). The SnapshotTree analogue of this is asserted (a symlink entry whose bytes hash to the digest is prereg_not_in_tree); the GitTree one is not.

mutations.name: GitTree.blob rejects a blob exactly at MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES
mutations.why: Moves the receipt cap one byte in the refusing direction: a blob of exactly 64 MiB, which the spec says is readable, becomes UNRESOLVED receipt_too_large. This is the cap boundary on the git path. A test would have to assert that a blob whose size equals sworn.MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES still resolves ok through GitTree, and that MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES + 1 does not. The SnapshotTree boundary is pinned at the cap (an at-cap entry is served); the GitTree side of the same boundary has no equivalent assertion, and materialising a 64 MiB fixture is exactly the kind of test nobody writes.

mutations.name: GitTree._index drops at-cap blobs from the prereg index
mutations.new: if len(parts) >= 3 and parts[1] == b"blob" and parts[2].isdigit() and int(parts[2]) < MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES:
mutations.old: if len(parts) >= 3 and parts[1] == b"blob" and parts[2].isdigit() and int(parts[2]) <= MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES:
mutations.why: The second half of the cap boundary, on the --batch-check filter that decides which blobs get hashed for prereg lookup. A prereg file of exactly MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES is silently never indexed, so `prereg:<its digest>` answers UNRESOLVED prereg_not_in_tree -- a WRONG reason, since the file is in the tree and is inside the cap. A test would have to commit a blob of exactly MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES and assert find_sha256 of its digest returns ok, not prereg_not_in_tree. Nothing distinguishes prereg_not_in_tree-because-absent from prereg_not_in_tree-because-wrongly-filtered today.

mutations.name: A missing git binary reports commit_absent instead of git_unavailable
mutations.new:
rc, out, err = self._git("cat-file", "-t", self.commit)
        if rc != 0 or out.strip() != b"commit":
mutations.why: _git() returns rc 127 when subprocess.run raises OSError -- no git binary, no such repo directory. Dropping the 127 branch collapses "I could not look" into "the commit is not there": the verifier claims a fact about the repository's contents that it never observed. Every span in the document flips from UNRESOLVED git_unavailable to UNRESOLVED commit_absent. Both are UNRESOLVED, so any test that only asserts the verdict passes; a test would have to assert the REASON string is git_unavailable when git cannot run (e.g. GitTree(nonexistent_path, "c"*40)._ready() == "git_unavailable"). This is precisely the reason-vocabulary distinction the layer owns and the JavaScript side never sees.

mutations.name: GitTree.find_sha256 stops lowercasing the prereg digest
mutations.why: The index is keyed by hashlib's lowercase hexdigest. Removing the .lower() normalisation makes an uppercase or mixed-case `prereg:ABCD...` receipt answer UNRESOLVED prereg_not_in_tree even though the file is committed at that digest -- a document that verifies as HELD today silently stops holding, with a reason that reads as an accusation about the tree. A test would have to run a prereg receipt with an UPPERCASE digest through GitTree and assert HELD. The uppercase-digest vector exists, but only against MemoryTree/SnapshotTree; every GitTree prereg case uses a lowercase digest.

mutations.name: SnapshotTree stops accepting executable-mode files as blobs
mutations.why: Narrows the blob-mode gate so mode 100755 -- an ordinary executable file, e.g. a committed script or a harness runner -- is UNRESOLVED not_a_blob in both blob() and find_sha256(). A receipt pointing at any executable file stops resolving, and a prereg body committed with the exec bit becomes invisible to digest lookup. GitTree, which gates on `type == blob` rather than an allowlist of modes, would keep answering ok, so the two handles silently disagree. A test would have to put a 100755 entry in a SnapshotTree and assert it resolves, or assert SnapshotTree agrees with GitTree on a fixture repo containing an executable file. Every mode used in the snapshot tests is 100644, 040000, 120000 or 160000.

mutations.name: SnapshotTree stops inferring size from embedded bytes
mutations.why: Removes the normalisation that derives an entry's size from the bytes actually embedded. An entry whose recorder omitted `size` but embedded bytes over MAX_RECEIPT_BYTES now leaves size as None, the cap comparison is skipped, and the oversized bytes are served ok -- the cap is bypassed entirely by omitting a field, and a snapshot vector can be crafted to make SnapshotTree read what GitTree would refuse as receipt_too_large. A test would have to construct an entry with "size": None and bytes longer than the cap (or a stubbed cap) and assert receipt_too_large. The existing cap tests all declare an explicit size.

mutations.name: A snapshot answers for a commit it was not taken at
mutations.why: Deletes the rule the class exists to enforce: a recorded tree may only answer for the commit its entries were read at. With the check gone, verify() overwrites the handle's commit with the DOCUMENT's commit, and a snapshot taken at commit A cheerfully serves its own bytes as the contents of commit B -- every span resolves HELD against a tree that was never at that commit, which is a fabricated verdict, not an UNRESOLVED one. A test would have to assert SnapshotTree(entries, A, commit=B).blob(path) == (None, "commit_absent"), including the case where the document supplies the mismatching commit. Note the surviving hex-format check still catches "HEAD" and uppercase ids, so a suite that only pins those forms would not notice.

mutations.name: MemoryTree.find_sha256 answers with no commit named
mutations.new:
def find_sha256(self, digest: str) -> Tuple[Optional[bytes], str]:
        for b in self.files.values():
mutations.why: Drops the no_commit refusal on the prereg path only, leaving blob() intact. A MemoryTree with commit=None -- a document that named no commit at all -- now resolves `prereg:<digest>` receipts to HELD while every path: receipt on the same document is UNRESOLVED no_commit. The verdict stops being a function of a named commit for one whole receipt form, and the two receipt forms of one document disagree about whether the tree is even addressable. A test would have to assert MemoryTree(files).find_sha256(d) == (None, "no_commit") specifically, or run a prereg document through a commit-less MemoryTree and expect UNRESOLVED.

mutations.name: sworn-span masking skips a span that starts at byte 0
mutations.why: The guard exists to skip spans with no canonical offsets (start is None on a lexically MALFORMED declaration). Weakened to a truthiness test, a span whose canonical start is exactly 0 — a document that opens with a sworn declaration, which is the overwhelmingly common shape — is no longer blanked out of the narrative. Its own sworn text then re-enters the sentence splitter, inflating narrative_sentences and DEFLATING sentence_share, and the sworn prose can itself be handed to claimdetect and reported back as an unsworn_claim. A test would have to verify a document whose FIRST byte begins a declaration and assert narrative_sentences (and that the sworn text does not appear in unsworn_claims); a document with any leading prose is unaffected.

mutations.name: fenced regions recomputed on raw canonical instead of the sworn-masked buffer
mutations.why: Fences are deliberately re-derived on the buffer AFTER sworn spans have been blanked, so a fence delimiter that lives inside a sworn span cannot toggle fence state. Reading the unmasked canonical instead, a ``` sequence inside sworn text flips the toggle and the whole fenced-region partition shifts by one: real narrative gets blanked and real fenced code gets counted as sentences. Silent and identical on every document where no sworn span contains a fence delimiter. A test would have to swear a span whose text contains a ``` line and assert narrative_sentences / sentence_share against the honest partition.

mutations.name: sentence splitter no longer breaks on newlines
mutations.why: Drops the \n+ alternation, so the splitter only breaks after terminal punctuation. Bullet lists, headings, and any unpunctuated line — precisely the shape of agent PR prose — collapse into one sentence, so narrative_sentences falls and sentence_share is flattered upward: the exact direction the v0.2 floor was redesigned to make impossible. The splitter is also the value advertised in cov["splitter"], which is now a lie about the regex actually used. A test would have to count sentences over newline-separated unpunctuated narrative, or compare the compiled pattern against diffgate's literal.

mutations.name: whitespace-only segments counted as narrative sentences
mutations.why: Masking replaces sworn and fenced bytes with 0x20, so the narrative is full of long all-space segments. The strip() test is what keeps those out of the count. Weakened to a plain emptiness test, every blank run becomes a 'sentence' with a text of '' handed to claimdetect, so narrative_sentences inflates by roughly the number of masked regions and sentence_share drops below the true floor — and empty strings appear in unsworn_claims spans. A test would have to assert narrative_sentences on any document that swears something or contains a fence.

mutations.name: sentence offsets stop excluding leading and trailing whitespace
mutations.old: sentences.append((a + lead, a + lead + len(seg.strip()), seg.strip()))
mutations.why: The recorded (start, end) is meant to be the canonical byte range of the sentence TEXT; here it becomes the range of the raw segment including its leading whitespace — which, after masking, is often a long run of blanked sworn bytes. Every entry in cov['unsworn_claims'] then points at a range that does not begin at the claim, so a reader slicing canonical[start:end] gets whitespace plus the wrong tail. The count and the share are unchanged, so only an offset-level assertion notices: a test would have to slice the canonical text at a reported claim's start/end and assert it equals the claim text.

mutations.name: 0/0 sentence_share reports a perfect floor instead of null
mutations.old: cov["sentence_share"] = (round(sworn_total / denom, 4) if denom else None)
mutations.why: The 0/0-is-null rule says a document with nothing sworn AND no narrative has no floor to report. Replacing null with 1.0 makes an empty document print coverage-floor≈1.00 in the CLI headline — the single most flattering number the instrument can emit, on the one input where it is meaningless. This is the same class of failure as the withdrawn v0.1 estimate. A test would have to verify b"" (or a document that is nothing but a fence) and assert sentence_share is None rather than a number.

mutations.name: sentence_share rounded to 2 digits instead of 4
mutations.why: The receipt's declared ROUNDING contract and the coverage block's 4-digit convention are what make coverage_reproduces a byte-for-byte comparison. At 2 digits, 1/3 prints 0.33 instead of 0.3333 and any receipt issued by a 4-digit verifier fails coverage_reproduces against this one — while the CLI headline, which formats to %.2f, looks completely unchanged. A test would have to assert sentence_share == round(x, 4) on a ratio whose 3rd/4th digits are non-zero, or re-verify a stored receipt's coverage block.

mutations.name: a lexically MALFORMED document is given a coverage floor instead of a refusal
mutations.why: This is the refusal: when the lexer produced no canonical text there is no narrative to measure, so the block returns with only a note and every count left null. Substituting an empty canonical lets the function run to completion: narrative_sentences becomes 0, and since a MALFORMED document still carries its declarations, denom == sworn_total > 0 and sentence_share prints 1.0. The CLI then headlines a document it just declared SWORN-FAILED / MALFORMED with coverage-floor≈1.00 and diff-claims≈0. A test would have to verify a document with invalid UTF-8 or unbalanced fences and assert narrative_sentences / sentence_share / diff_claim_sentences are all None.

mutations.name: an observer that raised publishes its partial count as if complete
mutations.why: 'the observer failing is not a verdict' — when claimdetect raises mid-scan the block deliberately discards everything it had and reports null, because a count taken over a prefix of the sentences is not a count. Publishing len(claims) turns a crash at sentence k into an authoritative diff_claim_sentences of however many claims happened to be found first, and the CLI prints it as diff-claims≈N with no indication it is a prefix (only the free-text note says 'raised'). A test would have to monkeypatch detect to raise partway through a multi-sentence document and assert diff_claim_sentences is None and unsworn_claims is empty.

mutations.control_reason: substitutes existing binding(s) n_sent - not a fresh local name
mutations.name: diff-claim share computed against the narrative denominator
mutations.why: diff_claim_share is defined against the STRUCT-1 count so it is readable beside diff_claim_sentences and labelled with the idiom it was measured on; sentence_share is the one measured against every narrative sentence. Swapping the denominator publishes two numbers under two labels that both mean the sentence floor, and diff_claim_share silently drops whenever a document has more sentences than STRUCT-1 flags (which is almost always, given STRUCT-1's documented blindness to result-shaped prose). A test would have to assert diff_claim_share == sworn/(sworn+diff_claim_sentences) on a document where the two counts differ.
